Methusael
mē-thū'sä-el
n. (the son of Mehujael and the father of Lamech, fourth in the line of Cain; not to be confounded with Methuselah in the line of Seth)
From Hebrew Methusha'el, commonly explained as man of God or who is of God, from math, a man, with El. The similar Methushelach — Methuselah, in the line of Seth — is a different name of a different man, though the resemblance has caused confusion since antiquity.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Methusael is the fourth and last quiet name in the line of Cain before the narrative stops to describe his son. “Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech” (Gen 4:18). Everything Genesis has to say about the house is said through that son. Lamech is the first polygamist in Scripture: “And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” (Gen 4:19) — a plain departure from the creation ordinance that a man shall cleave unto his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. From those two wives came the three culture-founders: “Adah bare Jabal: he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle” (Gen 4:20), Jubal the father of all such as handle the harp and organ (Gen 4:21), and “Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron” (Gen 4:22). And from the same house came the boast. Methusael's name, if it means man of God, sits in that setting with a heavy irony: four generations from a fratricide, in a family of real genius, a man is called of God, and his son sings about murder to his wives.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Methusael; in sacred history he is the son of Mehujael and the father of Lamech, in the line of Cain.

expand to see more

METHUSAEL, n. Man of God; a proper name in the fourth chapter of Genesis.

The son of Mehujael, and the fourth in descent from Cain.

He was the father of Lamech, who took unto him two wives.

He is not to be confounded with Methuselah, the son of Enoch in the line of Seth.

Of his own life the Scripture has recorded nothing.

Key Scripture

Gen 4:18 — "And unto Enoch was born Irad: and Irad begat Mehujael: and Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech."

Gen 4:19 — "And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah."

Gen 4:21 — "And his brother's name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ."

Gen 4:24 — "If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold."

Modern Corruption

Lamech's two wives are now often cited to argue that Scripture endorses a plurality of marriage forms. Genesis records polygamy first as a mark of the line of Cain and never once commends it; the creation ordinance is one man and one woman, and Christ says so.

expand to see more

The argument runs that since the Bible narrates polygamy without an explicit prohibition in Genesis, marriage in Scripture is culturally variable and the modern insistence on one man and one woman is a later imposition. The text will not support it. The first polygamist named in the Bible is Lamech, the son of Methusael, in the line of Cain, and he is introduced in the same breath as his song about killing a man. Every subsequent instance in Scripture — Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon — is narrated with its griefs attached: rivalry, contempt, exile, and in Solomon's case the loss of the kingdom to idolatry. Narration is not approval, and the Bible is not a book that only condemns in the imperative mood.

The standard is fixed at the creation and reasserted by Christ against every relaxation: “Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female” (Mat 19:4), and therefore “they twain shall be one flesh” (Mat 19:5) — two, not three, and a bond He calls unbreakable by man. Paul requires an elder to be the husband of one wife. The dictionary's position is the plain one: marriage is one man and one woman covenanting before God for life, and the household of Methusael's son is Genesis showing the reader the first departure from it, in the same chapter as the first murder.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Methusha'el (H4967), Methusael; math (H4962), man, men; El (H410), God; Lemek (H3929), Lamech; Tubal Qayin (H8423), Tubal-cain.

expand to see more

Hebrew Methusha'el (H4967) — Methusael; man of God, in the line of Cain.

Hebrew math (H4962) — man; the first element of the name.

Hebrew El (H410) — God; the closing element.

Hebrew Lemek (H3929) — Lamech; his son, the first polygamist named.

Hebrew Tubal Qayin (H8423) — Tubal-cain; his great-grandson, worker in brass and iron.

Usage

"“Methusael begat Lamech” — the last quiet name before the boast."

"“Lamech took unto him two wives” — the first departure from the creation ordinance."

"“The father of all such as handle the harp and organ” — art out of a violent house."
